title: Radiation effects, dose & ALARP
blurb: How ionising radiation harms cells, stochastic versus deterministic effects, typical dental doses and why every exposure is kept as low as reasonably practicable.
question: A worried parent asks whether their 9-year-old's two bitewings could cause cancer, and why the practice bothers with so many safety rules if the dose is small. How do you explain the risk honestly and simply?

teach.body: X-rays are ionising radiation. As they pass through the body they knock electrons out of atoms, creating charged particles and reactive free radicals. These can break or alter DNA. Most damage is repaired, some cells die, and occasionally a cell survives with a faulty copy of its DNA. That last outcome is what may, years later, lead to cancer. Dental doses are very small, but no dose is completely risk-free, so every exposure must be worth it.

steps.label: Ionisation
steps.sub: X-ray energy strips electrons from atoms

steps.label: DNA damage
steps.sub: Direct hits or free radicals break DNA

steps.label: Repaired
steps.sub: Most damage is fixed with no effect

steps.label: Cell dies
steps.sub: Large numbers dying cause tissue reactions

steps.label: Cell mutates
steps.sub: A rare survivor may later become cancerous

teach.caption: Steps 3 to 5 are the three possible outcomes for a damaged cell, not a sequence.
Deterministic effects are also called tissue reactions.
Bars show the top of each published range (FGDP/CGDent Selection Criteria, 2018). A periapical is up to about 3.5 days of natural background radiation; a panoramic no more than about 6 days.

teach.body: Young people's cells divide quickly and they have more years ahead for a cancer to develop, so the same dose carries more risk for a child than for an adult. That is why the guidance asks for particular care when justifying radiographs for children. For the parent in the scenario, the honest answer is that the risk from two bitewings is extremely small, comparable to a few days of natural background radiation, and is outweighed by finding decay early.

items.label: dose constraint used when planning dental X-ray rooms
where dental staff doses should sit: well below this

teach.caption: Dose limits do not apply to patients. Patients are protected by justification and optimisation under IR(ME)R 2017 instead.

teach.h: ALARP: as low as reasonably practicable
teach.body: Because stochastic risk has no safe threshold, the aim is to keep every dose as low as reasonably practicable (ALARP) while still getting a diagnostic image. For patients this is called optimisation. In practice it means rectangular collimation, receptor holders, the right exposure setting, fast digital receptors and good technique. A retake doubles the dose for that view, so getting it right first time is one of the most effective protection measures a nurse contributes to.

teach.text: Stochastic = chance (cancer), NO threshold, dose changes the PROBABILITY. Deterministic = certain above a THRESHOLD, dose changes the SEVERITY. Dental radiography only carries a stochastic risk.

items: Ionising radiation can damage DNA directly or through free radicals.
Stochastic effects (cancer) have no threshold; deterministic effects (burns, cataract) need a high threshold dose.
Dental doses are tiny: an intraoral film is up to about 3.5 days of background radiation.
Children are more radiosensitive. Every exposure must be justified and kept ALARP; retakes add dose.

summary: You can now explain how ionising radiation damages cells, tell stochastic from deterministic effects, put dental doses into perspective against background radiation, quote the IRR17 dose limits, and explain why ALARP and avoiding retakes matter.

A.q: Which effect of radiation has no safe threshold, with the chance of it occurring rising as dose increases?
A.why: Cancer is a stochastic effect: there is no threshold, and higher dose raises the probability rather than the severity.

whyNot.0: Skin reddening is deterministic and only occurs above a threshold dose.
whyNot.1: Cataract is a deterministic tissue reaction with a threshold.
whyNot.3: Burns are deterministic and need doses far above anything used in dentistry.

A.q: A periapical radiograph gives a dose roughly comparable to which of the following?
options: A few days of natural background
A full year of background radiation
A hospital CT scan of the chest
Less than one second of background
A.why: Guidance puts a periapical at up to about 3.5 days of UK natural background radiation.

whyNot.1: A year of background is about 2,230 µSv, far more than an intraoral image.
whyNot.2: Medical CT doses are many times higher than any intraoral view.
whyNot.3: Even the lowest intraoral doses are more than a second's worth of background.

A.q: What is the annual whole-body dose limit for members of the public under IRR17?
A.why: IRR17 sets a whole-body limit of 1 mSv per year for members of the public.

whyNot.0: 20 mSv is the limit for employees aged 18 and over.
whyNot.1: 0.3 mSv is a dose constraint used in planning, not the legal public limit.
whyNot.2: 6 mSv is the limit for trainees under 18, not the public.

B.q: Why is a child's radiograph given extra care when it is being justified?
B.why: Children's dividing cells and longer life expectancy make them more sensitive to the stochastic risk of radiation.

whyNot.0: Children usually need lower exposure settings because they are smaller.
whyNot.2: Thyroid collars are not the reason; collars are not routinely used for anyone.
whyNot.3: Absorption by teeth is not the issue; sensitivity of the child's tissues is.

B.q: A colleague says a retake 'doesn't matter because the dose is tiny'. Which response best reflects ALARP?
options: Retakes are fine if the patient agrees
Retakes only matter for panoramic films
Retakes are needed for every audit
B.why: ALARP means avoiding any dose that isn't needed; a retake repeats the whole exposure, so good first-time technique protects the patient.

whyNot.0: Patient agreement does not make an avoidable dose acceptable.
whyNot.1: Every view, intraoral or extraoral, adds dose when repeated.
whyNot.3: Audits review existing images; they never require extra exposures.

B.q: Which of these is a deterministic (tissue reaction) effect of radiation?
B.why: Cataract is a tissue reaction that only occurs above a threshold dose, with severity increasing as dose rises.

whyNot.0: Leukaemia is a cancer, a stochastic effect.
whyNot.2: Thyroid cancer is stochastic, which is why the thyroid is kept out of the beam.

C.q: What does ALARP stand for in radiation protection?
options: Average level of accepted radiation protection
C.why: ALARP means as low as reasonably practicable: doses kept as low as possible while still achieving the purpose.

whyNot.1: This is a made-up phrase, not the legal principle.
whyNot.2: This is not what the acronym stands for.
whyNot.3: ALARP is not an average or an accepted level.

C.q: Ionising radiation damages cells mainly by:
options: Heating the tissue it passes through
Blocking blood supply to the cell
C.why: Ionisation breaks or alters DNA, directly or via free radicals, which can kill a cell or cause mutation.

whyNot.0: Diagnostic doses deposit far too little energy to heat tissue.
whyNot.2: Radiation does not work by blocking blood vessels.
whyNot.3: Cell membranes are not dissolved; the key target is DNA.

C.q: Which radiographic examination generally gives the HIGHEST effective dose?
C.why: Small-field CBCT ranges from about 11 to 214 µSv, well above intraoral, panoramic or ceph doses.

whyNot.0: A bitewing is an intraoral view at 0.3–21.6 µSv.
whyNot.1: A lateral ceph is about 2.2–14 µSv.
whyNot.2: A periapical is in the same low intraoral range as a bitewing.

reteach.title: Lottery tickets and sunburn
reteach.question: How can one kind of radiation harm be like buying lottery tickets, and another like getting sunburnt?

blocks.body: Stochastic effects are like lottery tickets. Every exposure is another ticket. Each one has a tiny chance of 'winning' (a cancer), and more tickets mean a bigger chance, but a winning ticket isn't worse because you bought more. Deterministic effects are like sunburn: below a certain amount of exposure nothing happens, but beyond it everyone burns, and more exposure means a worse burn. Dental X-rays never get near the 'sunburn' level, so the only concern is not buying unnecessary tickets.

blocks.text: Every unnecessary exposure, including a retake, is an extra 'ticket'. That's the whole logic of ALARP.

explain.body: X-rays ionise atoms, forming free radicals and breaking DNA. A damaged cell either repairs itself, dies, or survives with a mutation. Mutated survivors are what may lead to cancer years later.

test.q: Which outcome of radiation damage to a cell is linked to cancer?
options: The cell survives with altered DNA
test.why: A cell that survives with mutated DNA can later multiply abnormally, which is how radiation-induced cancer arises.

whyNot.0: Full repair leaves no lasting effect.
whyNot.2: A dead cell cannot become cancerous.
whyNot.3: An unaffected cell carries no added risk.

explain.body: Stochastic effects (cancer, heritable effects) are chance events with no threshold; dose changes the probability. Deterministic effects (burns, cataract, hair loss) occur above a threshold and get more severe with dose.

test.q: For a deterministic effect, what happens as the dose increases above the threshold?
test.why: Above the threshold, a deterministic effect gets worse as dose increases.

whyNot.0: Higher dose never makes an effect less likely.
whyNot.2: Above the threshold the effect occurs; it does not stop.
whyNot.3: Effects don't switch category with dose.

explain.body: Intraoral views are 0.3–21.6 µSv, a DPT 2.7–38 µSv and small-field CBCT 11–214 µSv. UK background is about 2,230 µSv a year, so a periapical is up to about 3.5 days of background.

items.label: background equivalent of a DPT (at most)

test.q: A patient asks how a panoramic radiograph compares with everyday radiation. Which is the most accurate answer?
options: No more than about six days
test.why: Guidance compares a panoramic radiograph to no more than about 6 days of UK natural background radiation.

whyNot.0: A year of background is many times a DPT dose.
whyNot.1: A month greatly overstates the dose.
whyNot.3: Less than an hour understates even the lowest DPT doses.

explain.body: Keep doses as low as reasonably practicable: rectangular collimation, holders, correct settings, digital receptors, and good technique so images don't need retaking. Staff dose limits exist, but patients are protected by justification and optimisation instead.

steps.label: Justified?
steps.sub: Only if the benefit outweighs the risk

steps.label: Optimised
steps.sub: Lowest dose for a diagnostic image

test.q: Which of these does NOT help keep patient doses ALARP?
options: Taking a spare image just in case
test.why: An extra 'just in case' image is an unjustified exposure and adds dose with no benefit.

whyNot.0: Rectangular collimation halves dose compared with a round beam.
whyNot.1: Holders improve positioning and reduce retakes.
whyNot.2: Correct settings avoid both excess dose and unusable images.
